steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid)

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group on the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA: Ribose (has an –OH on the 2′ carbon).  
   Result: RNA is more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G).  
   • RNA: Adenine (A), Uracil (U) replaces thymine, Cytosine (C), Guanine (G).

3. Strandedness & shape  
   • DNA: Usually double-stranded; forms a long, antiparallel, right-handed double helix (B-form in cells).  
   • RNA: Usually single-stranded; can fold back on itself to create complex secondary/tertiary structures (hairpins, loops, stems).

4. Length & size  
   • DNA: Genomic DNA molecules can be millions of base pairs long.  
   • RNA: Individual RNA molecules are typically much shorter (tens to thousands of nucleotides).

5. Location (eukaryotic cells)  
   • DNA: Confined mainly to the nucleus (and small amounts in mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
   • RNA: Synthesized in the nucleus but functions mainly in the cytoplasm (and in organelles); some RNAs remain nuclear.

6. Stability  
   • DNA: Very stable; suitable for long-term genetic storage.  
   • RNA: Relatively unstable; degraded quickly by ubiquitous RNases; fits its role as a transient messenger/regulator.

7. Function  
   • DNA: Long-term storage of hereditary information; template for its own replication and for transcription into RNA.  
   • RNA:  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries genetic code to ribosomes.  
     – Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) forms core of ribosomes.  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA) delivers amino acids during translation.  
     – Regulatory RNAs (siRNA, miRNA, lncRNA, etc.) control gene expression.  
     – Catalytic RNAs (ribozymes) perform enzymatic reactions.  
     – Telomerase RNA, viral genomes, etc.

8. Replication & synthesis  
   • DNA replicates via DNA polymerases, needs primers, occurs during S phase.  
   • RNA is synthesized (transcribed) from DNA by RNA polymerases; no replication in normal cells except for some RNA viruses.

9. Repair mechanisms  
   • DNA has elaborate proofreading and repair systems (mismatch, excision, recombination repair).  
   • RNA generally is not repaired; instead it is degraded and resynthesized.

10. Genetic coding in viruses  
   • Many viruses use RNA as their genetic material (e.g., SARS-CoV-2, HIV); some are double-stranded, others single-stranded.  
   • Cellular organisms universally store genomes in DNA.

11. Chemical labeling conventions  
   • DNA bases often abbreviated dATP, dGTP, etc. (d for deoxy).  
   • RNA bases: ATP, GTP, etc. (no “d”).

12. Experimental handling  
   • DNA is easier to work with; more resistant to nucleases and pH.  
   • RNA requires stringent RNase-free techniques; alkaline solutions quickly hydrolyze RNA due to 2′-OH–mediated cleavage.

Mnemonic summary  
DNA: Double-stranded, Deoxy sugar, Durable, Data archive.  
RNA: Ribose, Reactive, (usually) single-stranded, Rapidly turned over, Regulators/enzymes/messengers.

Bottom line  
DNA is the stable, double-stranded, deoxyribose-based repository of genetic information. RNA is the versatile, generally single-stranded, ribose-containing molecule that copies, expresses, regulates, and sometimes even stores (in viruses) genetic information, but usually in a transient, easily replaceable form.
